title: What are idempotent methods, and which HTTP methods are idempotent (and why)?
shortTitle: What are idempotent methods, and which HTTP methods are idempotent (and why)

s1_definition.oneliner: An HTTP method is idempotent when making the same request once or many times leaves the server in the same final state, so it is safe to retry.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Idempotent** – sending the identical request one time or many times produces the same server-side state; the response may differ, but the effect is identical.
- **GET, HEAD, OPTIONS** – idempotent because they only read and never change state.
- **PUT** – idempotent because it fully replaces a resource; the second write overwrites with the same values.
- **DELETE** – idempotent because the resource ends up deleted whether you delete it once or ten times.
- **POST** – not idempotent because each call typically creates a new resource, so two identical POSTs create two resources.
- **PATCH** – not guaranteed idempotent because a relative change like "add 100 to balance" stacks on repeats.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine Rajesh presses an elevator button at National Bank of India. Pressing it once or ten times calls the elevator to the same floor: that is idempotent. Now imagine a "transfer 50,000 rupees" button. Pressing it ten times moves 500,000 rupees: that is not idempotent and it is dangerous. Idempotent actions are the ones where repeating the press changes nothing extra, so if Rajesh is not sure whether the first press registered, he can press again without fear.

sections.s6_takeaway:
An HTTP method is idempotent when sending the same request one time or many times leaves the server in the same final state. The important detail is that idempotency is about server state, not the response, so a DELETE that returns 204 the first time and 404 the second is still idempotent because the resource ends deleted either way. The idempotent methods are GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, PUT, and DELETE, while POST and PATCH are generally not idempotent.

The reasoning behind each is straightforward. GET, HEAD, and OPTIONS only read, so repeating them changes nothing. PUT is a full replacement, so writing the same complete representation twice ends in the same state. DELETE leaves the resource gone whether called once or ten times. POST is not idempotent because it normally creates a new resource each time, and PATCH is not idempotent in general because a PATCH like "add one hundred to the balance" would stack up on repeats.

The reason this matters in a banking system is retries under unreliable networks. At National Bank of India, when Rajesh tapped Transfer on a weak signal and the response timed out, his app could not tell whether the money had moved. If the transfer endpoint were a plain POST, that retry would have created a second transfer and moved fifty thousand rupees twice. Because POST is not idempotent by the specification, the team added an idempotency key: the client sends a unique key in a header, the server records it, and a repeat of the same key returns the original transfer instead of executing a new one.

In practice, idempotent methods like GET, PUT, and DELETE can be retried freely by intermediaries and background jobs, while POST endpoints that move money or have side effects need an Idempotency-Key to become safely retryable. That combination keeps the system both resilient to network failures and correct about never double-charging a customer.

Remember one sentence: idempotency means the same request produces the same server state no matter how many times you send it, and it is what makes retries safe.

---

keyPoints: An idempotent method produces the same server-side state whether called once or many times.
GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, PUT, and DELETE are idempotent; POST and PATCH are generally not.
Idempotency is defined by server state, not the response body, so a DELETE returning 404 on retry is still idempotent.
POST is not idempotent because each call typically creates a new resource, risking duplicates on retry.
The Idempotency-Key header retrofits idempotency onto POST by storing and returning the result of the first call.
Proxies and retry libraries rely on idempotency to decide whether to automatically retry a failed request.
